# الملحق 6-ز: سكربت اختبار BM25 الموسع

> مصدر حرفي من القرص: `/home/hatch/workspace/goals/wiki-to-rag-conversion-for-six-personas/files/bm25_rich_test.py` — 3512 بايت، 74 سطراً (بعدّ الأسطر). لم يُعدَّل حرف واحد.

[BEGIN VERBATIM]

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Stdlib-only BM25 check on Haitham Talaat: 20 largest pages AND all 210 pages.
Usage: python3 bm25_rich_test.py
No installs, no keys, read-only on the wiki dir. Same BM25 params as
bm25_test_20.py (k1=1.2, b=0.75, title+front-matter+body, Arabic word regex).
Queries: 8 title-derived + 7 paraphrases, each with a known target page."""
import glob, math, os, re
from collections import Counter

BASE = os.path.expanduser("~/workspace/yt-wiki/wikis/haitham-talaat/wiki/pages")

def load(paths):
    docs = []
    for p in paths:
        txt = open(p, encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore").read()
        docs.append((os.path.basename(p), re.findall(r"[\w\u0600-\u06FF]+", txt.lower())))
    return docs

def rank_of(docs, q, exp):
    toks = re.findall(r"[\w\u0600-\u06FF]+", q.lower())
    n = len(docs)
    avg = sum(len(t) for _, t in docs) / n
    df = Counter()
    for _, t in docs:
        for w in set(t):
            df[w] += 1
    out = []
    for name, t in docs:
        c = Counter(t)
        sc = 0.0
        for w in toks:
            if w in c:
                idf = math.log(1 + (n - df[w] + 0.5) / (df[w] + 0.5))
                f = c[w]
                sc += idf * (f * 2.2) / (f + 1.2 * (1 - 0.75 + 0.75 * len(t) / avg))
        out.append((sc, name))
    ranked = [nm for _, nm in sorted(out, reverse=True)]
    return ranked.index(exp) + 1, ranked[:3]

TESTS = [
    ("الملحد في الغرب صورة الملحد المجتمعات الغربية", "src-wdDmYOzNdTE.md"),
    ("مناظرة أدلة الوجود رياض الخزرجي الرودسين", "src-yg8OEx-hKrg.md"),
    ("أميرة بنت حمد علاج الطاقة قتل الطفلة", "src-xy3WWY4QD6s.md"),
    ("مخطوطات السيرة ابن هشام ابن إسحاق", "src-x_zZ9GueF0c.md"),
    ("طوفان نوح غمر الأرض كلها", "src-yXFLgX47R0E.md"),
    ("أندرو تيت علمانية تسامح زائف", "src-BxqCzBJo1Fk.md"),
    ("الكهانة التاروت توقعات ليلى عبد اللطيف", "src-Bl3bdTPBNgk.md"),
    ("جدل التطور غياب دليل أحفوري انتقال كائن", "src-2f-gNvuXy7k.md"),
    ("لماذا الغرب لا يحترم الملحدين", "src-wdDmYOzNdTE.md"),
    ("دليل العين والرودسين إثبات وجود الله", "src-yg8OEx-hKrg.md"),
    ("امرأة قتلت ابنتها بسبب التأمل الطاقي", "src-xy3WWY4QD6s.md"),
    ("هل توجد مخطوطات أصلية للسيرة النبوية", "src-x_zZ9GueF0c.md"),
    ("هل الطوفان غمر كل الأرض", "src-yXFLgX47R0E.md"),
    ("ما حكم التاروت والأبراج في الإسلام", "src-Bl3bdTPBNgk.md"),
    ("لماذا لا يوجد دليل أحفوري على التطور", "src-2f-gNvuXy7k.md"),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    allf = sorted([(os.path.getsize(p), p) for p in glob.glob(BASE + "/*.md")])
    corpora = [
        ("20-largest", [p for _, p in sorted(allf, reverse=True)[:20]]),
        ("all-210", [p for _, p in allf]),
    ]
    for label, paths in corpora:
        docs = load(paths)
        r1 = top3 = 0
        print(f"\n== {label} n={len(docs)} bytes={sum(os.path.getsize(p) for p in paths)}")
        for q, exp in TESTS:
            r, top = rank_of(docs, q, exp)
            r1 += r == 1
            top3 += r <= 3
            print(f"rank {r:3d}  {q} -> {exp}  top3={top}")
        print(f"rank1: {r1}/{len(TESTS)}  top3: {top3}/{len(TESTS)}")

[END VERBATIM]

## نص فيديو: 4SB3T1reCHw.en.txt

[BEGIN VERBATIM]

Hey everyone. Today we're diving into
one of the most exciting innovations in
AI knowledge management, the LLM Wiki
pattern introduced by Andrej Karpathy in
April 2024. This is going to completely
change how you think about organizing
and accessing your knowledge. If you've
ever uploaded a PDF to chat GPT, asked a
question, and then uploaded the same PDF
again the next day, you already
understand the problem we're solving
today. Let me paint you a picture.
You're researching electric vehicles.
You upload three PDFs to chat GPT. One
about Tesla's battery technology, one
about charging infrastructure, and
another about EV market trends. You ask,
"How does Tesla's battery compare to
industry standards?" Chat GPT gives you
an answer. Great. But here's the thing.
Tomorrow, when you ask, "What are the
main barriers to EV adoption?" the
system starts from zero. It rereads
everything. It rediscovers the same
information. Nothing from yesterday's
session carries over. This is the
fundamental with retrieval augmented
generation, or rag. Every query is
independent. Knowledge doesn't compound.
It's like having amnesia every single
day. Before we go further, let's talk
about who came up with this solution.
Andrej Karpathy is a co-founder of
OpenAI, former director of AI at Tesla,
where he built the autopilot neural
network stack, and honestly, one of the
best teachers of deep learning concepts
in the world. In April 2024, he
published a simple GitHub gist that went
viral in the developer community within
days. It wasn't a product. It wasn't
code. It was a pattern, a way of
thinking about knowledge management that
changes everything. Karpathy uses a
brilliant analogy from software
engineering, compilation. When you write
code, you don't execute the source code
directly every time. First, a compiler
transforms it into an optimized binary.
That compilation step is expensive, but
it pays for itself across every
subsequent use. The LLM Wiki works the
same way. Your raw documents are like
source code. The compilation process is
when the LLM reads them and builds a
structured Wiki. The Wiki is your
optimized binary, preprocessed,
cross-referenced, ready to query. You
compile once, query forever. Instead of
rereading raw documents every time, you
build a persistent structured knowledge
base that gets smarter with every new
source you add. The LLM Wiki has three
cleanly separated layers. Let me break
this down. Layer one, the sources. This
is your intake layer. Research papers,
articles, meeting notes, YouTube
transcripts, anything you want the
system to learn from. These live in a
sources or raw directory and are treated
as immutable. The LLM reads them, but
never modifies them. Layer two, the
Wiki. This is where the magic happens.
The LLM reads your sources and creates
structured Wiki pages, one per concept,
person, or topic. Each page has
summaries, cross-references using Wiki
links, and provenance tracking showing
which sources contributed to it. Layer
three, the schema. This is your
clawed.md file. It's like a contract
between you and the AI. It defines what
types of pages exist, what structure
they should follow, and how the LLM
should maintain the Wiki. Think of it
this way. Obsidian is the IDE. The LLM
is the programmer, and the Wiki is the
code base. Let's see this in action with
a real example. You're building a Wiki
about AI research. Step one, you drop a
PDF about transformer architecture into
your sources folder. Step two, you tell
Claude Code, or your AI agent, "Ingest
this new source." Step three, the LLM
reads the entire document and gets to
work. It creates a new page called
transformer architecture with a summary.
It creates or updates a page for
attention mechanism. It updates the
author page for Viswani et al. It finds
connections. Oh, this relates to the
BERT page I created last week, and adds
cross-links. It tracks which source
contributed what information. The
critical difference, this is permanent.
Next time you ask about transformers,
the LLM doesn't reread the PDF. It reads
your already compiled, cross-referenced
Wiki page. And when you add a new paper
about BERT, the system updates the
existing transformer page to include new
insights.
Let's directly compare RAG with the LLM
Wiki pattern. With RAG, every query
searches raw documents from scratch. No
accumulation of knowledge between
sessions. Slow. Has to reprocess the
same content repeatedly. Struggles to
connect information across multiple
documents. Good for one-off questions.
With LLM Wiki, queries navigate a
pre-built structured knowledge base.
Knowledge compounds. Each new source
makes the entire Wiki smarter. Fast. The
compilation happened once up front.
Excellent. It synthesizes across all
your sources. Gets better over time.
Imagine asking, "What are the
philosophical connections between Rich
Sutton's AI work and Andrej Karpathy's
teaching approach?" In RAG, the system
searches through papers and blog posts
trying to piece together an answer on
the fly. In LLM Wiki, you already have a
Rich Sutton page, an Andrej Karpathy
page, and a philosophy of AI research
page that links both. The connections
are already drawn. The answer is instant
and synthesized. Here's what makes this
truly revolutionary, the compounding
principle. Every time you add a new
source, the entire Wiki gets smarter,
not just a new file in a database. The
whole system evolves. Let's say your
Wiki has 50 pages about machine
learning. You add a new paper about a
breakthrough in optimization. The LLM
updates the optimization concepts page,
revises the neural network training page
to mention this new technique, flags a
potential contradiction with an older
paper, creates links from gradient
descent and learning rate schedules,
updates the author's page with this new
publication, and here's the kicker,
there's a dash-save flag. When you ask a
question and the LLM synthesizes a
valuable new insight, that answer gets
automatically filed as a new Wiki page.
Future sessions benefit immediately.
Your questions literally improve the
Wiki. Knowledge compounds. This is the
shift from stateless retrieval to
stateful growing intelligence. All
right, let's talk about how to actually
build this. You need three main tools.
Tool one, Obsidian. This is a free
markdown editor that works on your local
files. Why Obsidian? Three killer
features. Wiki links. Use wikit link to
link between pages. Graph view.
Visualize your entire knowledge base as
a connected network. Local first. Your
data lives on your computer, not in the
cloud. Tool two, Claude Code. This is
Anthropic's command-line AI agent. It
can read and write files directly on
your computer. Think of it as the brain
that maintains your Wiki. Tool three,
your sources. PDFs, markdown files, web
articles, anything you want to learn
from. The system handles text natively.
Now, if you're not comfortable with
command-line tools, don't worry. There
are no-code alternatives like Doomco
work that replicate this workflow with a
simple interface. But for developers,
Claude Code gives you the full power.
Let me show you how this works in
practice with some actual code. First,
you create your directory structure.
Then, you create a clawed.md schema
file. This tells the LLM what your Wiki
should look like. Here's a simple Python
function that shows the compilation
process. And this is how you query the
Wiki. Notice a few things. The
compilation step is expensive. It reads
everything and writes structured pages.
The query step is cheap. It just
searches already processed content.
Embeddings help find relevant pages, but
the Wiki structure does most of the
work. Where does this actually shine?
Let me give you some real-world
scenarios. Research. PhD students
maintaining literature review Wikis.
Every paper they read updates their
understanding of the field. By the time
they write their dissertation, they have
a complete cross-referenced knowledge
base. Product management. A PM
maintaining a Wiki of customer feedback,
feature requests, and market research.
New customer interviews automatically
update existing concept pages about pain
points. Legal work. Law firms building
case Wikis. Every brief, deposition, and
precedent gets compiled into a
searchable, linked knowledge base.
Junior associates can query senior
partners' institutional knowledge.
Personal learning. Someone learning
about philosophy, history, or science.
Books, podcasts, articles, all feed into
a growing Wiki that helps them see
connections they'd never find manually.
Anywhere knowledge builds over time,
this pattern fits perfectly. One of
Karpathy's brilliant additions is the
lint operation. Just like code linters
catch bugs, the Wiki lint catches
knowledge bugs. Orphan pages, Wiki pages
that no other page links to, missing
pages, concepts mentioned in Wiki links
that don't have their own page yet,
broken cross-references, links pointing
to non-existent pages, contradictions,
conflicting information from different
sources, stale embeddings, pages that
aren't in your vector index anymore. You
run lint periodically, and the LLM gives
you a health report. Then, you can ask
it to fix issues automatically, like
create the missing concept pages, or
resolve the contradiction about battery
lifespan. This is maintenance you'd
never do manually at scale. The LLM does
it consistently. How does this compare
to tools you might already use.
Notion/Rome, great for manual
note-taking. LLM Wiki, the AI does the
writing and linking for you. Notebook
LM/ChatGPT file uploads, good for quick
questions on uploaded files. LLM Wiki,
knowledge persists and compounds across
sessions. Traditional RAG systems, good
when sources rarely change. LLM Wiki,
better when you're continuously learning
and adding sources. Enterprise knowledge
bases, require dedicated teams to
maintain. LLM Wiki, self-maintaining,
scales with one person. The LLM Wiki
isn't replacing these tools. It's a
different paradigm. It's for knowledge
that builds and evolves, not static
reference material. Let's be real about
the limitations. Limitation one, initial
setup cost. Compiling a large source
base takes time and compute. If you have
a hundred PDFs, that first pass might
take hours. But remember, you do it
once. Limitation two, LLM errors. The
LLM might misunderstand sources, create
hallucinated connections, or structure
pages incorrectly. You need to review,
especially early on. Limitation three,
not real-time. This isn't Google. It's
not searching the web. It's compiling
your sources. For breaking news or
real-time info, this isn't the right
tool. Limitation four, technical
barrier. The original implementation
requires comfort with command line
tools, Git, and Obsidian. That said,
no-code alternatives are emerging. These
limitations are real, but for the right
use case, deep accumulating knowledge
work, the benefits far outweigh the
costs. Ready to build your first LLM
Wiki? Here's a step-by-step plan. Step
one, choose your topic. Start narrow. AI
research, project management frameworks,
Roman history, not everything I've ever
read. Step two, gather five to ten
sources. PDFs work best. Articles and
markdown, also great. Start small. You
can always add more. Step three, set up
Obsidian. Create a vault. Create three
folders, sources, wiki, and a claw.md
file. Step four, write your schema.
Define what types of pages you want. For
a research wiki, concept, author, paper
summary, method. Step five, paste
Carperpediem's original gist into Claude
code and ask it to help you set up the
process. It'll walk you through the
process. Step six, ingest your first
source. Watch the magic happen as pages
get created and linked. Step seven,
query your wiki. Ask synthesis questions
that span multiple sources. Step eight,
keep adding sources. Watch your wiki
grow denser and smarter. Your first wiki
might be rough. That's fine. The system
improves as you use it. Start small,
iterate, and let it grow organically.
Where is this pattern going? I see three
major directions. Direction one, no-code
tools. Products like Doom Co-work are
making this accessible to
non-developers. Drag and drop files,
watch your wiki build. No terminal
required. Direction two, collaborative
wikis. Right now, this is personal, but
imagine teams maintaining shared wikis.
Every meeting transcript, every document
updates a collective knowledge base.
Direction three, multimodal wikis. Today
it's text, tomorrow videos, images,
audio. Imagine your wiki compiling
YouTube lectures, podcast transcripts,
and research papers into one unified
knowledge graph. Carperpediem's insight
that knowledge should compound, not
evaporate, is going to influence how we
build AI tools for years to come. We're
at the very beginning. Let's wrap up
with the key ideas. Takeaway one, RAG is
stateless. Every query starts from
scratch. LLM Wiki is stateful. Knowledge
compounds. Takeaway two, think
compilation, not retrieval. Build the
structure once, query it forever.
Takeaway three, three layers. Immutable
sources, AI-maintained wiki, and a
schema that guides the LLM. Takeaway
four, your role shifts. Instead of
organizing knowledge manually, you
curate sources and ask questions. The
LLM handles maintenance. Takeaway five,
this works best for deep accumulating
knowledge work, research, learning,
professional expertise. The difference
between RAG and LLM Wiki is like the
difference between Googling every time
you need information versus building a
second brain that actually remembers and
connects ideas. And that's LLM Wiki, a
pattern that transforms how we build,
maintain, and query personal knowledge
bases. If you want to try this, check
the links in the description for
Carperpediem's original gist, download
Obsidian and Claude code, start with
five documents on a topic you're
passionate about, give yourself a
weekend to experiment. I guarantee
you'll never look at RAG the same way
again. If this video helped you
understand LLM Wiki, hit that like
button and subscribe for more deep dives
into AI patterns and tools. Drop a
comment telling me what you're planning
to build your first wiki about. I read
every single one. Thanks for watching,
and I'll see you in the next video.
Happy compiling.

[END VERBATIM]

مهم للنماذج مفتوحة المصدر
كجزء من الكوكبة هنا.
وكما تعلمون، أعتقد أننا تأخرنا
في التصرف بشأن ذلك،
لكننا سنفعل ذلك جيدًا الآن.
CA: أعني، يبدو أنك تنفقه، مثل أمر،
أو حتى أوامر بحجم أكبر مما
يُزعم أن DeepSeek أنفقته،
على الرغم من أنني أعلم
أن هناك جدلًا حول ذلك.
هل أنت واثق من أنه سيتم التعرف
على النموذج الفعلي الأفضل؟
أم أنك في الواقع مثل،
أليس هذا يهدد الحياة من بعض
النواحي لفكرة أنه، نعم،
من خلال نطاق واسع، عشرات
المليارات من الدولارات من الاستثمار،
يمكننا الحفاظ على صدارة مذهلة.
SA: دوما، أتصل بالناس وأتوسل إليهم أن
يقدموا لنا وحدات معالجة الرسومات لهم.
نحن مقيدون للغاية.
نمونا يسير على هذا النحو.
تم إطلاق DeepSeek، ولا يبدو أنه يؤثر عليه.
هناك أشياء أخرى تحدث.
CA: أخبرنا عن النمو، في الواقع.
لقد أعطيتني رقمًا
صادمًا وراء الكواليس هناك.
SA: لم يسبق لي أن رأيت نموًا في أي
شركة، شركة شاركت فيها أم لا،
مثل هذا، مثل نمو ChatGPT.
إنه ممتع حقًا.
أشعر بالفخر والشرف العميق.
لكن من الجنون العيش فيه،
وفرقنا منهكة ومتوترة.
ونحن نحاول الحفاظ على الأمور.
CA: كم عدد المستخدمين لديك الآن؟
SA: أعتقد أن آخر مرة قلنا
فيها كانت 500 مليون نشاط أسبوعي،
وهي تنمو بسرعة كبيرة.
CA: أعني، أخبرتني أن هذا الضعف تضاعف
في غضون أسابيع قليلة.
كما هو الحال من حيث الحوسبة أو من حيث...
SA: قلت ذلك بشكل خاص، ولكن أعتقد...
كاليفورنيا: أوه.
(ضحك) أخطأت
في التذكر يا سام، أنا آسف.
يمكننا تحرير ذلك من الشيء
إذا كنت تريد ذلك حقًا.
ولن يقوم أحد هنا بتغريدها.
SA: إنها تنمو بسرعة كبيرة.
(ضحك) CA:
إذن أنتم واثقون، ترونها تنمو، تقلع
مثل سفينة الصواريخ،
تطلقون نماذج جديدة مذهلة طوال الوقت.
ما الذي تراه في أفضل
النماذج الداخلية لديك الآن
والذي لم تشاركه بعد مع العالم
ولكنك ترغب في التواجد هنا في هذه المرحلة؟
SA: أولاً وقبل كل شيء، سألت عن،
هل نحن قلقون بشأن هذا النموذج أو ذاك؟
سيكون هناك الكثير من النماذج
الذكية في العالم.
سيتم تحويل النماذج الذكية جدًا
إلى سلعة إلى حد ما.
أعتقد أنه سيكون الأفضل،
ولبعض الاستخدامات، سترغب بها.
ولكن بصراحة، أصبحت
النماذج الآن ذكية جدًا لدرجة
أنه بالنسبة لمعظم الأشياء
يريد  الناس القيام بها،
فهي جيدة بما يكفي.
آمل أن يتغير ذلك بمرور الوقت
لأن الناس سيرفعون توقعاتهم.
ولكن مثل، إذا كنت تستخدم
ChatGPT كمستخدم قياسي،
فإن قدرة النموذج ذكية جدًا.
لكن علينا أن نبني منتجًا رائعًا،
وليس مجرد نموذج رائع.
وبالتالي سيكون هناك الكثير من الأشخاص
الذين لديهم نماذج رائعة،
وسنحاول بناء أفضل منتج.
والناس يريدون جيل الصور الخاص بهم، كما
تعلمون، رأيت بعض أمثلة
سورا للفيديو في وقت سابق.
إنهم يريدون دمجها مع جميع
الأشياء الخاصة بهم.
لقد أطلقنا للتو ميزة
جديدة، لا تزال تسمى الذاكرة،
لكنها أفضل بكثير من الذاكرة السابقة،
حيث سيتعرف عليك هذا النموذج
على مدار حياتك.
ولدينا الكثير من الأشياء
التي يجب أن نبنيها
مثل هذا المنتج المتكامل الرائع.
وكما تعلمون، أعتقد أن الناس سيلتزمون بذلك.
لذلك سيكون هناك العديد
من النماذج، لكنني أعتقد أننا
سنواصل، كما آمل، التركيز على بناء
أفضل منتج محدد في هذا المجال.
CA: أعني بعد أن رأيت إعلانك بالأمس
أن ChatGPT سيعرف كل
سجل الاستعلام الخاص بك،
أدخلت «أخبرني عني،
ChatGPT، من كل ما تعرفه.»
وسقط فكي يا سام، كان الأمر صادمًا.
لقد عرفت من أنا وكل
هذه الأنواع من الاهتمامات
التي نأمل أن تكون في الغالب
مناسبة جدًا وقابلة للمشاركة.
لكنها كانت مذهلة.
وشعرت بإحساس الإثارة الحقيقية،
ببعض الغثيان،
ولكن بشكل أساسي الإثارة،
في الواقع، إلى أي مدى
سيسمح ذلك بأن يكون مفيدًا لي.
SA: قام أحد باحثينا بالتغريد، كما تعلمون،
نوعًا ما مثل الأمس أو هذا الصباح،
أن التحميل يحدث شيئًا فشيئًا.
ليس كما تعلم، أنك تسد عقلك في يوم واحد.
لكنك ستتحدث إلى ChatGPT
على مدار حياتك وفي يوم
من الأيام، ربما إذا
أردت، سوف يستمع إليك طوال اليوم
ويراقب ما تفعله نوعًا ما، وسيتعرف
عليك وسيصبح هذا الامتداد
لنفسك، هذا الرفيق، هذا الشيء الذي يحاول
فقط، مثل، مساعدتك على أن تكون الأفضل،
وتبذل قصارى جهدك.
CA: في فيلم «Her»
، تعلن منظمة العفو
الدولية أساسًا أنها قرأت جميع
رسائل البريد الإلكتروني الخاصة
به وقررت أنه كاتب رائع وكما
تعلمون، تقنع الناشر بنشره.
قد يأتي ذلك في وقت أقرب مما نعتقد.
SA: لا أعتقد أن ذلك سيحدث
بالضبط على هذا النحو، ولكن نعم،
أعتقد شيئًا في الاتجاه
حيث الذكاء الاصطناعي - ليس
عليك فقط، مثل، الذهاب
إلى ChatGPT أو أي شيء آخر
والقول، لدي سؤال، أعطني إجابة.
لكنك تحصل على أشياء
مدفوعة بشكل استباقي تساعدك،
تجعلك أفضل أو أي شيء آخر.
يبدو أن هذا قريبًا.
CA: إذن ما الذي رأيته قادمًا، داخليًا،
والذي تعتقد أنه سيفجر عقول الناس؟
أعطنا تلميحًا على الأقل
عن ماهية قطارة الفك الكبيرة التالية.
SA: الشيء الأكثر حماسًا
بالنسبة لي شخصيًا هو الذكاء
الاصطناعي للعلوم في هذه المرحلة.
أنا من أشد
المؤمنين بأن أهم محرك للعالم ولحياة الناس
التي تتحسن أكثر فأكثر
هو الاكتشاف العلمي الجديد.
يمكننا أن نفعل المزيد من الأشياء
بموارد أقل، فنحن نوعًا
ما نتراجع عن حدود ما هو ممكن.
لقد بدأنا نسمع الكثير من العلماء
بأحدث نماذجنا
التي تفيد بأنها في الواقع أكثر
إنتاجية مما كانت عليه من قبل.
هذا في الواقع مهم لما يمكنهم اكتشافه.
CA: ما هو الاكتشاف المعقول على المدى
القريب، مثل درجة حرارة الغرفة -
SA: الموصلات الفائقة؟
CA: الموصلية الفائقة، نعم.
هل هذا ممكن؟
SA: لا أعتقد أن قوانين الفيزياء تمنع ذلك.
لذلك يجب أن يكون ممكنًا.
لكننا لا نعرف على وجه اليقين.
أعتقد أنك ستبدأ في رؤية بعض...
تقدم ملموس ضد المرض باستخدام
الأدوات المدعومة بالذكاء الاصطناعي.
ربما تستغرق
الفيزياء وقتًا أطول قليلاً،
لكنني آمل ذلك.
لذلك هذا مثل اتجاه واحد.
شيء آخر أعتقد أنه كبير سيبدأ قريبًا جدًا،
كما الحال خلال أشهر.
لقد تم بالفعل تحويل
تطوير البرمجيات بشكل كبير.
يبدو أنه من المدهش تمامًا مدى
اختلاف عملية إنشاء البرامج الآن
عما كانت عليه قبل عامين.
لكنني أتوقع خطوة أخرى بهذا الحجم
في الأشهر المقبلة
حيث تبدأ هندسة البرمجيات
الوكيلة في الحدوث حقًا.
CA: لقد سمعت المهندسين يقولون إنهم
مروا بلحظات تشبه
اللحظات الدينية تقريبًا مع بعض
النماذج الجديدة حيث يمكنهم
أن يفعلوا خلال
بعد الظهر ما كان سيستغرقه عامين.
SA: نعم، إنه مثل العقل -
يبدو تلك كانت أحد لحظاتي الكبيرة
في «الشعور بالذكاء الاصطناعي العام».
CA: لكن تحدث عن الشيء
الأكثر رعبًا الذي رأيته.
لأنه، كما هو الحال
في الخارج، يتصورك الكثير من الناس، كما
تعلمون، لديك حق الوصول إلى هذه الأشياء.
ونسمع كل هذه الشائعات الصادرة عن الذكاء

إلهي، لقد رأوا الوعي»،
أو «لقد رأوا الذكاء
الاصطناعي العام»، أو «لقد رأوا نوعًا
من نهاية العالم
قادمة.» هل رأيت، هل كانت هناك
لحظة مخيفة عندما رأيت شيئًا داخليًا
وفكرت، «آه أوه، نحن بحاجة إلى الاهتمام
بهذا؟» ج: كانت هناك لحظات من الرهبة.
وأعتقد أن هذا دائمًا
ما يكون مثل، إلى أي مدى سيذهب هذا؟
ماذا سيكون هذا؟
ولكن لا يوجد مثل، ليس لدينا سرًا،
فنحن لا نجلس سرًا على نموذج واعي أو شيء
قادر على تحسين الذات
أو أي شيء من هذا القبيل.
كما تعلمون، أنا...
لدى الناس وجهات نظر مختلفة جدًا
حول مخاطر الذكاء الاصطناعي الكبيرة.
وأنا شخصياً تطورت في التفكير
في المكان الذي سنراه فيه.
ما زلت أعتقد أنه
ستأتي نماذج قوية جدًا يمكن
للناس إساءة استخدامها بطرق كبيرة.
يتحدث الناس كثيرًا عن احتمالية
ظهور أنواع جديدة من الإرهاب البيولوجي،
والنماذج التي يمكن أن تمثل
تحديًا حقيقيًا للأمن السيبراني،
ونماذج قادرة على تحسين الذات
بطريقة تؤدي إلى نوع من فقدان السيطرة.
لذلك أعتقد أن هناك مخاطر كبيرة هناك.
ثم هناك الكثير من الأشياء الأخرى،
والتي بصراحة هي نوع ما أعتقده،
يقصده الكثير من الناس،
حيث يتحدث الناس عن المعلومات المضللة
أو النماذج التي تقول أشياء
لا تعجبهم أو أشياء من هذا القبيل.
CA: بالتمسك بالأول،
هل تتحقق من ذلك داخليًا قبل الإصدار؟
SA: بالطبع، نعم.
لذلك لدينا إطار الاستعداد هذا
الذي يحدد كيفية القيام بذلك.
CA: أعني، لقد تعرضت لبعض حالات
الخروج من فريق السلامة الخاص بك.
كم عدد الأشخاص الذين غادروا، لماذا غادروا؟
SA: لدينا، لا أعرف الرقم الدقيق،
ولكن من الواضح وجهات نظر
حول أنظمة السلامة بالذكاء الاصطناعي.
أود حقًا أن أشير إلى سجلنا الحافل.
هناك أشخاص سيقولون كل أنواع الأشياء.
كما تعلمون، ما يقرب من 10 في المئة
من العالم يستخدم أنظمتنا الآن كثيرًا.
ونحن فخورون جدًا بسجل السلامة.
CA: لكن السجل الحافل ليس
المشكلة بطريقة ما -
SA: لا، إنه كذلك.
CA: لأننا نتحدث عن قوة متنامية بشكل كبير
حيث نخشى أننا قد نستيقظ يومًا
ما وينتهي العالم.
لذا فإن الأمر لا يتعلق حقًا بالسجل الحافل،
بل يتعلق بالقول المعقول إن القطع موجودة
لإغلاق الأشياء بسرعة إذا رأينا خطرًا.
SA: نعم، لا، بالطبع، هذا مهم بالطبع.
لا تحب أن تستيقظ يومًا ما وتقول
: «مرحبًا، لم تكن لدينا أي عملية أمان.
الآن نعتقد أن النموذج ذكي حقًا.
لذا علينا الآن الاهتمام بالسلامة».
عليك أن تهتم بها طوال هذا المنحنى الأسي.
بالطبع تزداد المخاطر، وهناك تحديات كبيرة.
لكن الطريقة التي نتعلم
بها كيفية بناء أنظمة آمنة
هي هذه العملية التكرارية
لنشرها في العالم، والحصول
على التعليقات، في
حين أن المخاطر منخفضة
نسبيًا، والتعرف على مثل
هذا، هذا شيء يتعين علينا معالجته.
وأعتقد أنه مع انتقالنا
إلى هذه الأنظمة الفعالة،
هناك فئة كبيرة كاملة من الأشياء
الجديدة التي يجب أن نتعلم معالجتها.
CA: لنتحدث عن أنظمة الوكلاء والعلاقة
بين ذلك وبين الذكاء الاصطناعي العام.
أعتقد أن هناك ارتباكًا،
أنا في حيرة من أمري.
لذا فإن الذكاء العام الاصطناعي،
يبدو أن ChatGPT هو بالفعل ذكاء عام.
يمكنني أن أسأله
عن أي شيء، ويعود بإجابة ذكية.
لماذا ليس هذا الذكاء الاصطناعي العام؟
SA: لا...
أولا، لا يمكنك أن تطلب منه أي شيء.
من اللطيف منك قول ذلك،
هناك الكثير من الأشياء
التي لا يزال الأمر سيئًا فيها بشكل محرج.
ولكن حتى لو قمنا
بإصلاحها، وهو ما نأمل أن نفعله،
فإنها لا تتعلم وتتحسن باستمرار.
لا يمكن أن تتحسن في شيء
ضعيف فيه حاليًا.
لا يمكنها الذهاب لاكتشاف العلوم
الجديدة وتحديث فهمها والقيام بذلك.
كما أنه لا يستطيع نوعًا
ما، حتى لو خفضنا الشريط،
لا يمكنه القيام بأي عمل معرفي
يمكنك القيام به أمام الكمبيوتر.
أنا في الواقع، حتى بدون هذا النوع من
القدرة على التحسن
في شيء لا يعرفه حتى الآن، قد
أقبل ذلك كتعريف لـ AGI.
لكن الأنظمة الحالية، لا
قد تقول، مرحبًا، اذهب
وقم بالمهمة من أجل وظيفتي،
وتنطلق وتنقر على الإنترنت
وتتصل بشخص ما وتنظر إلى ملفاتك وتقوم بذلك.
وبدون ذلك، يبدو الأمر بالتأكيد أقل من ذلك.
CA: أعني، هل لديكم داخليًا تعريفًا
واضحًا لما هو الذكاء الاصطناعي العام،
ومتى تعتقدون أننا قد نكون هناك؟
SA: إنها مثل النكتة،
إذا كان لديك 10 باحثين من OpenAI في غرفة
وطلبت تعريف الذكاء الاصطناعي
العام، فستحصل على 14 تعريفًا.
CA: هذا مثير للقلق، أليس كذلك؟
نظرًا لأن هذه كانت المهمة في البداية،
«سنكون أول من يصل إلى AGI.
سنفعل ذلك بأمان.
لكن ليس لدينا تعريف واضح لما هو عليه».
SA: كنت سأنهي الإجابة.
كاليفورنيا: آسف.
SA: لكن ما أعتقد أنه مهم،
وما يريد الناس معرفته ليس أين
توجد هذه اللحظة
السحرية، كما تعلمون، «لقد انتهينا».
ولكن بالنظر إلى أن ما يبدو
أنه سيحدث هو أن النماذج
ستصبح أكثر ذكاءً وأكثر
قدرة وأكثر ذكاءً وأكثر قدرة،
في هذه الفترة الأسية
الطويلة، سيطلق عليها
أشخاص مختلفون اسم الذكاء
الاصطناعي العام في نقاط مختلفة.
لكننا نتفق جميعًا على أن الأمر
سيتجاوز ذلك بكثير.
كما تعلمون، إلى أي شيء
تريد تسميته بهذه الأنظمة
التي تصبح أكثر قدرة منا بكثير.
الشيء المهم هو كيف نتحدث عن نظام
آمن من خلال كل هذه الخطوات وما بعدها،
حيث يصبح النظام أكثر قدرة منا،
حيث يمكن للنظام القيام
بأشياء لا نفهمها تمامًا.
وأعتقد أن الأمر الأكثر أهمية من موعد ظهور
الذكاء الاصطناعي العام وما هو
تعريفه، هو إدراك أننا
في هذا المنحنى الأسي المذهل.
ويمكنك، كما تعلمون، أن تقول أن هذا هو
ما أعتقد أن الذكاء الاصطناعي العام هو.
يمكن القول تعتقد هذا ما تعتقده
بشأن الذكاء الاصطناعي العام.
يمكن لشخص آخر أن يقول إن
الذكاء الفائق موجود هنا،

Karpathy's LLM Wiki just went insanely
viral. And once you understand what it
actually does, you'll see why. Andrej
Karpathy, one of the original minds
behind Tesla's self-driving AI and a
founding member of OpenAI, dropped a
tweet about how he's been using AI to
build personal knowledge bases. Racked
up thousands of likes and shares in
hours. Over 5,000 stars on GitHub in
days. But why did it blow up? Because he
solved a problem that every single
person running a business quietly
struggles with. Information piles up,
right? Research piles up. Notes go
everywhere. And when you're running an
agent or you're trying to get contacts
with anything that you're using with AI,
you can't find it. You can't use this
knowledge, right? And the AI struggles
with it, too. So, this is Karpathy's
answer to that problem, and it's not
complicated. Here's the core idea. Most
AI tools, for example, Notebook LM,
ChatGPT, file uploads, standard rag
systems, they retrieve. You ask a
question, the AI goes hunting through
your documents, grabs some chunks, and
assembles an answer. Then the next time
you ask something, it does the whole
thing again from scratch. Nothing
compounds, nothing builds, and context
is very hard to get right inside the AI
agent, even if you give them a memory
and D file to OpenClaw or Claude Code,
etc., they still struggle with
retrieving good information that's
actually useful. Karpathy's approach is
different. Instead of just retrieving,
the AI compiles. You drop a document in,
and the AI reads it,
documents it, extracts what matters, and
weaves it into a living wiki, a
structured collection of interlinked
markdown files that gets richer time you
add something new. Cross-references
already built. Contradictions already
flagged. Synthesis already done. You ask
your question once, and the answer gets
filed back into the wiki. The next time,
the answer's already there, better,
faster, and with more context. That's
the shift. It goes from retrieval to
accumulation.
Now, most people have no idea how much
time they're wasting re-researching
things they already researched last
month. Think about how you actually
work. Right now, you might read an
article about a competitor. You save it
to your bookmarks. 3 weeks later, you
need it, but you can't find it. Or you
paste it into ChatGPT, get an answer,
close the tab, and it's gone. Your
research doesn't compound. You start
from zero every single time. Karpathy's
system fixes that. And here's how it
actually works in practice. So, there's
three layers. Layer one is your raw
resources, right? So, articles, PD
screenshots, research papers, anything
you want to pull from. And these are
untouched. The AI just reads them, but
never changes them. Layer two is the
wiki itself, a folder of markdown files
the AI builds and maintains. Entity
pages, concept pages, summaries,
comparisons, an overview that updates
itself. You read it, the AI writes it.
Layer three is the schema, a document
that tells the AI exactly how to
maintain the wiki, what conventions to
follow, how to ingest new sources, what
to do when there's a contradiction.
Think of it as the operating manual the
AI runs on. And you co-build this with
the AI over time. The IDE Karpathy uses
is Obsidian. He has the AI agent open on
one side, Obsidian on the other. The AI
makes changes, he browses the results in
real time. He describes it like this.
The LLM is the programmer, the wiki is a
code base, and Obsidian is the IDE.
If you're running a consultancy, an
agency, or any business where you do
deep research on clients or markets,
picture having a wiki that already knows
everything you've ever researched. New
client comes in, you feed the AI a few
sources about their industry, and the
wiki updates. Competitive intel,
summaries, connections to things you
researched 6 months ago, all there,
already linked together. Here's the part
that really matters. When you ask the
wiki a complex question, the AI doesn't
reread your raw documents. It reads the
already compiled wiki pages, which are
designed to answer exactly that kind of
question. Karpathy says, "At around 100
articles and 400,000 words, the AI
handles it without needing fancy
infrastructure. No embeddings, no vector
databases, just well-maintained index
files and the AI reading them
intelligently. And the outputs aren't
just text in a chat window." Karpathy
has the AI render markdown files,
slideshows in map format, and charts.
You can pipe the outputs straight into
Obsidian, and they get filed back into
the wiki. So, every question you ask
makes the knowledge base smarter. And
that right back loop is where the
compounding really kicks in. There was
actually someone who commented back to
him after his viral tweet, Chris from
bits of Chris.com, and he said he's been
running a version of this against 4,000
personal journal entries and research
notes over 2 years. His finding is that
the right back mechanic is the single
most important part. The explorations
should grow the knowledge base just like
new sources do. Every insight, every
connection the AI finds, file it back
in. The wiki learns from your thinking,
not just from your sources. He also
found something important about scale.
At 100 articles, an auto-maintained
index works fine. At thousands of messy
notes, you need a bit more. He uses a
technique called overfetch and rerank.
Pull three times as many results as you
need, strip out near duplicate content,
then rerank for diversity. The
difference, he says, is night and day.
Inside the AI Profit Boardroom right
now, we've got a 30-day roadmap built
specifically around using AI agents like
this to systematically capture research,
automate knowledge workflows, and build
the kind of compound intelligence that
gives you an edge over competitors who
are still copying and pasting into
ChatGPT. There's 2,700 members in there,
a lot of them running research-heavy
service businesses, content operations,
client work, already implementing AI
knowledge systems. You get four weekly
coaching calls every week walking you
through exactly how to set this up in
your business. Link in the comments and
description, or just go to the AI Profit
Boardroom.com. Now, here's where it gets
interesting, because people in the

different directions Karpathy didn't
even mention. One builder created Swarm
Vault, a TypeScript CLI that implements
the whole pattern end to end. Ingest,
compile, query, lint with a knowledge
graph that tracks confidence-scored
connections between concepts and flags
which nodes have the most connections.
It's open source. It works with OpenAI,
Anthropic, Gemini, and our local models.
Another builder, going by a Sachin on
GitHub, has been running a version as
his personal operating system for
months. A few of his additions also
worth paying attention to, too. So, he
dropped the central index file entirely.
Instead of maintaining one master index,
the AI scans summaries and tags at query
time. He says this scales better, and
nothing goes stale. The index becomes a
liability as the wiki grows. Distributed
metadata beats a central list. He added
decision learning loops. Every decision
has an outcome section you fill in
later. So, when you're making a new
decision, the AI surfaces past decisions
and what actually happened. The system
literally learns from your history. Good
calls get reinforced. Bad calls become
constraints. He built in a training
period, 30 days, where the system asks a
lot of questions, learns your
preferences and conventions, and then
quiets down and just implements. The
wiki trains its own AI. And he added
context optimization. The system
periodically reviews its own instruction
files for bloat, suggests splitting
overloaded pages, and compacts with your
approval, which is self-maintaining.
Here's what's underneath all of this,
and I want to make sure you don't miss
it. The reason this matters for your
business is not the technology itself.
The technology is just markdown files in
an AI with good instructions. The reason
it matters is that most people running
businesses are carrying their expertise
in their heads with scattered notes
across browser tabs and Slack threads
and forgotten bookmarks. The person who
builds a compounding knowledge base has
an advantage that grows every week. The
person without one is researching the
same things on a loop. I've noticed a
pattern with the people moving fastest
right now in agencies, in content
businesses, in consulting. They're not
just using AI to answer questions.
They're using AI to build systems that
hold knowledge and then querying those
systems for decisions. The knowledge
compounds. The decisions get better. The
competitive gap widens. This becomes
more important as we become more
agentic. For example, OpenClaw is 10
times better when it understands you,
who you are, and your business context.
Karpathy's wiki pattern went viral
because it named something people have
been feeling, but couldn't articulate.
We don't just need faster search, we
need knowledge that accumulates. And the
really interesting version of this, the
one Karpathy hints at at the end of his
gist, is what happens when the wiki gets
big enough that you fine-tune a model on

research, your frameworks, your

that thinks the way your business
thinks. And that's coming, right? And

Subnormal. Subnormal intelligence
represents the most limited form of
human cognitive function. People at this
level may have an IQ below 70, often due
to genetic conditions like Down
syndrome, brain injury, or complications
during development. They usually
struggle with language, memory, and
abstract thinking. Simple tasks like
dressing, feeding, or understanding
basic instructions may require
assistance for life. Their experience of
the world is immediate and sensory. They
respond more to tone and touch than to
logic or language. Emotional recognition
can still be strong. They often sense
kindness, fear, or frustration in
others. While they may never live
independently, many form deep emotional
bonds and express joy, sadness, or
connection in profound non-verbal ways.
Modern society emphasizes care, respect,
and inclusion over outdated or offensive
labels. With love, structure, and
support, people at this level can live
meaningful lives within their capacity.
Below average Below average intelligence
includes individuals who can function
independently, but tend to struggle with
complex reasoning or abstract thinking.
IQ scores typically range from 70 to 85.
People in this group may find academic
subjects like math, science, or grammar
difficult, and they often learn better
through repetition and hands-on
activities than through theory or
abstract instruction. They might work
best in structured environments with
clear routines, such as jobs involving
manual labor, customer service, or
caregiving. While they may lag behind in
formal education, many have strong
practical or interpersonal skills.
Socially, they may be outgoing, loyal,
and emotionally intuitive. This level of
intelligence is often overlooked or
underestimated. But with the right
support, people here can live
independently, raise families, and
contribute meaningfully to their
communities. They thrive when respected
for what they can do rather than judged
for what they can't. Average. Most
people live here, and most think they
don't. Average intelligence enables
people to read, write, do math, follow
rules, and hold conversations. You
understand cause and effect, make plans,
and learn from mistakes. It's the
intelligence of routines, relationships,
and basic problem solving. You grasp
what needs to be done and usually get it
done. Teachers, drivers, small business
owners, nurses, technicians, they're all
here. The world doesn't run without
average intelligence. It's balanced,
functional, and enough to adapt. But
here's the catch. This level feels like
the end of growth. People here are often
smart enough to think they understand
everything, but not sharp enough to see
their blind spots. They confuse being
right with being informed, and they
rarely ask deeper questions. Because
life works the way it is. This level is
stable, but also sticky. It traps the
most people, not because they're
incapable of growth, but because they
never feel the need to try. Above
average. Above average intelligence is
where thought gets fast. You don't just
learn, you leap. You spot patterns
others miss. You see outcomes forming
long before others even realize there's
a problem. School may have felt slow,
repetitive. Conversations sometimes feel
like waiting in line. These minds do
well in theoretical fields, math,
coding, engineering, philosophy. They
enjoy complexity, puzzles, systems. But
there's a shadow to it. You see too much
too early. You might talk less because
you're editing yourself mid-sentence.
You might fake normaly just to keep the
peace. This level breeds frustration not
because others are stupid but because
they're not fast enough to sink. And if
you're not careful, high intelligence
becomes high detachment. You float above
the noise but forget how to be human in
it. High high intelligence typically
refers to IQ's between 130 and 145,
about the top 2% of the population.
People at this level don't just learn
quickly. They often make intuitive
leaps, seeing solutions before others
even identify the problem. They excel at
recognizing patterns, thinking
abstractly, and mastering complex
systems. In school, they might breeze
through advanced material or teach
themselves topics far beyond the
curriculum. They often enjoy logic
puzzles, deep discussions, and solitary
research. Many are drawn to fields like
theoretical science, software
engineering, or philosophy, areas that
reward abstract and strategic thinking.
Emotionally, they may feel isolated or
misunderstood, especially during youth
when their cognitive speed outpaces
their emotional development. When
supported, however, they become
innovators and problem solvers who push
boundaries. High intelligence isn't just
being smart. It's being able to think in
ways most people can't even imagine.
Gifted. This is where exceptional
ability begins to truly stand out. Often
marked by IQ's above 145. But it's more
than numbers. Gifted individuals process
the world with rare speed, depth, and
originality. From an early age, they may
show strong memory, laser focus, and the
ability to connect big ideas across
different subjects. They might teach
themselves piano, build machines from
junk, or write novels before high
school. They don't just solve problems,
they reframe them. Their thinking can be
unconventional, insightful, and years
ahead of their age. But giftedness can
come with challenges, frustration with
slow systems, isolation from peers, or
intense emotions that are hard to
manage. Their minds are fast, but so are
their feelings. When supported, they
become the innovators, creators, and
deep thinkers who stretch the limits of
human knowledge and imagination.
Genius. Genius intelligence isn't just
about being smart. It's a different
architecture. Geniuses don't just solve
problems. They rebuild the logic beneath
them. They don't master rules. They
question why the rules exist. Think
Einstein. Think Rammanujan. Think people
whose brains don't just run faster, they
run sideways. This level brings
breakthroughs. Entire paradigms shift
when these people speak. Science,
philosophy, art all get redefined. But
genius doesn't feel like a gift to the
person who holds it. It often feels like
isolation at the speed of light. People
can't keep up. Institutions can't
accommodate. Even praise feels like a
mistransation. And most of the time,
geniuses are punished before they're
praised. Too radical, too strange, too
soon. Polymath. Polymaths are geniuses
with range. While a typical genius might
master one field, a polymath masters
many. They might be inventors, writers,
scientists, and artists all in one
lifetime. Historical examples include
Leonardo da Vinci, who designed
machines, painted masterpieces, and
studied anatomy. Benjamin Franklin, who
helped shape science, politics, and
printing. What defines this level is a
brain that doesn't just absorb
knowledge. It synthesizes it across
disciplines. Polymaths don't see
subjects as separate. They find patterns
linking math to music or biology to
philosophy. Their curiosity is endless
and their creativity thrives on variety.
Polymath intelligence demands more than
raw IQ. It requires time, discipline,
and a deep love of learning. These
individuals often work across decades.
Driven by questions no single field can
answer. In a world that pushes
specialization, polymaths remind us of
the power of thinking broadly.
Visionary. People with visionary
intelligence don't just understand the
world. They imagine what it could
become. Their intelligence is part
genius, part foresight, and part
courage. While a polymath masters many
fields, a visionary sees beyond existing
systems entirely. They introduce ideas
that seem impossible until they change
everything. Visionaries connect the dots
between science, society, and spirit.
They see what others miss, then take the
leap to build it. This level of
intelligence often comes with risk.
Visionaries challenge norms, face
rejection, and endure doubt. But they
persist, powered by belief and boldness.
Their thinking shapes industries,
movements, and history itself. Visionary
intelligence isn't just about being
smart. It's about using that brilliance
to bend the future. Transcendent.
Transcendent intelligence is the highest
level of all. At this point,
intelligence stops being about answers.
It becomes about awareness. These minds
don't just connect dots. They question
the dots themselves. They see through
ego, through systems, through thought.
They sense patterns in human nature,
cycles in consciousness, illusions in
identity. Think Buddha, Jung, Socrates.
Visionaries who didn't just know. They
understood why we crave knowing.
Transcendent intelligence isn't shiny.
It's quiet. Still, often mistaken for
madness. Because it threatens everything
we build our sense of self on. These
people don't dominate. They dissolve.
They guide without pushing. At this
level, intelligence stops serving the
self. It starts serving truth. I'll be
making more videos like this soon.
Subscribe to see them.

So, you set up your local AI. It runs
without breaking a sweat, and every
single session you feed it the same
context again, who you are, what you are
building, where things live, every time,
from scratch. So, you think, "Fine, I
will bolt on a memory system." And that
is where it falls apart. Most of them
eat too many resources, live in the
cloud, or your local model just is not
sharp enough to call the right tool at
the right moment. And no, rag is not the
answer here. I will get to why. Here is
the real problem. Almost every memory
system is built for frontier models, the
ones that follow a tool spec even when
you hand them half-baked instructions.
Andre Karpathy floated the idea of an
LLM wiki. Google standardized something
close with OK F, but asking a regular
local model to follow that spec to the
letter, while also doing the actual job
you gave it, is a huge ask. You are
diluting its intelligence across too
many things at once. So, I tried to move
the memory burden off the AI and onto
the tool itself. One dead simple tool
built on Karpathy's LLM wiki and
Google's OK F. And spoiler, it did not
go as smoothly as I thought. So, did it
work? What broke when I ran it on my own
local stack? And can this actually
become permanent memory for a local AI
setup? Let's find out. First, why not
just use rag? Rag is great when your
knowledge base is basically fixed,
terabytes that barely change, and you
want fast answers. But the intelligence
of the model is never used during
retrieval. It is vector math similarity
matching. That is the trade you make for
fast lookups out of huge data. A
text-based LLM wiki is different. It
behaves like actual memory. It reads one
file, and from there another, following
links until it lands on the exact thing
you need. And we are not storing
terabytes. We are storing personal
context, the stuff the AI decides is
worth remembering. That is constantly
changing. So, you do not want to
re-chunk and re-embed everything every
time one fact updates. If you have ever
used a coding agent, you know this
works. It follows breadcrumbs through a
code base like a detective. My first
attempt was the obvious one. A skill
file that embeds the OKF spec plus
instructions telling the AI where the
root of the memory folder is. It kind of
worked and it kind of did not. The model
ignored the root path, created the
folder in the wrong place, and forgot to
update the index. The concept is fine
when you have a Claude Opus level model.
A local model just cannot follow
instructions with that precision. So, is
it over? Not so fast. We just have to
get more creative. We solved this in
real life a long time ago. We store
human knowledge in libraries and every
library has a librarian. You ask a
question, the librarian finds it. You
have no idea what index the place uses.
You do not need to. That is the shape we
use. A library that stores the memories
and a librarian agent that takes a
query, finds the answer, and hands it
back. When new knowledge comes in, the
librarian files it away so it turns up
next time. In technical terms, memory
indexed at every level, an index file
the model can walk, and links between
the files so it jumps to the right
section. And the system is
deterministic. The rules are fixed. It
only calls the model when it genuinely
has to make a decision, so we never
drift off the spec. I also added a web
UI to talk to the librarian directly and
a graph visualizer of how the memories
link. Because if it is easy to
visualize, it is easy to debug. Now, I
need my other AI systems to plug in and
use this as their memory layer. That
comes down to a handful of MCP tools.
Query gives the librarian read tools
only. Update memory adds edit, so a
stale fact gets fixed. Add memory adds
write, so anything worth keeping folds
into an existing file or becomes a new
one. And because the librarian handles
all of that, I never bloat my actual
agents with the OKF spec or a pile of
memory rules. The librarian is an agent,
so it needs a brain. It connects to the
same llama.cpp
server everything else in my stack
already uses, auto discovers whatever
model is loaded, sits behind llama swap
two, and prefers it. So, a memory query
never triggers a swap. Think about that.
The harness, the memory, and the model.
The whole loop runs on my own box. No
cloud API anywhere in the chain. This
thing is truly local. Okay, on paper it
was done. Then I plugged the real client
model in over MCP, and that is exactly
where it broke. It had a kind of amnesia
it did not know it had. All the client
could see was the tool names, query,
add, update, status. So, when you asked
it something, it answered straight from
its own head. It never checked the
memory first because it had no idea it
held anything useful. And the irony is
the internal agent was fine the whole
time. We had been feeding it an overview
of the knowledge base in its system
prompt. It was the client model on the
other end of the wire flying blind. So,
the fix was to give it a reason to look
first. The moment a session connects, we
generate a seed memory, a small live
summary of what is in the base, and push
it through the two channels that reach
the client at startup. The MCP
instructions field and the description
of the query tool. Now, the model opens
every session already knowing there is a
segment on billing, one on people, one
on infrastructure. It stops guessing and
starts querying. And we made the seed
list what each concept is about, not
file names, because your question is far
more likely to match 100 requests per
minute than a file called rate
limits.md. Once it was reliably writing
to memory, a subtler problem showed up.
It treated memory like a junk drawer.
Every new fact became its own file. I
tell it, I live in Hyderabad, and it
spins up a standalone Hyderabad file
disconnected from the profile about me
that already exists. The memory grew,
but none of it connected. A pile of
nodes, not knowledge. So, I gave it two
rules. First, enrich before you create.
Search for the concept this fact belongs
to, and if it is just an attribute of
something that exists, patch it in. Do
not spawn a new file. Second, link both
ways. When it genuinely is a new thing,
create the concept, then patch the
related ones, too. So, my profile says
runs the channel, and the channel says
created by me. One honest note on the
model. I first tried this with Gemma,
the 12B. Mechanically, it was fine, but
on the agentic side, the decisions about
what to enrich and what to link, it kept
getting wrong. So, I went back to my
trusty Quinn 3, the 30BA3B,
and I watched it on a single consumer
GPU do exactly this on its own. Enrich
the small facts, wire up the big ones,
no hand-holding. By now, the memory was
behaving, but I had a feeling I was
reinventing a wheel someone smarter had
already drawn. So, I went back to what
Karpathy actually laid out, and a couple
of things were still missing. First,
graph health. I added a lint step, fully
deterministic, that walks every link and
flags orphans, concepts nothing points
to, and broken links, pointers that go
nowhere. One catch that mattered. The
auto-generated index files had to be
excluded as link sources, or everything
looks connected and orphan detection is
useless. Then a maintain tool acts on
it, and an internal agent wires the
orphans back into the concepts they
relate to. Orphans went from one to zero
on its own. And contradictions. If I say
I moved from Hyderabad to Bangalore, the
old version would just append Bangalore
and leave Hyderabad sitting in the file.
The fix was mechanical. The old fact has
to be gone everywhere. Rewrite the whole
file if you have to. After that, it
cleanly said Bangalore, and only
Bangalore. And here's the part that
actually landed. Because it all runs
through the MCP layer, every agent I use
shares the same memory. Whichever tool I
am in, it already knows what happened in
the other one. My projects, the tool I
prefer, the IP of my local box, without
me repeating myself every session. It
became the memory of my AI, the thing I
use every day now. I do not reintroduce
myself anymore, but I will be honest.
This is not finished, and that is my
favorite part. Next up is a cache layer,
a hot tier of your most recent memories
the agent keeps close. So, it never digs
through the whole library just to recall
what happened 5 minutes ago. After that,
the one I'm excited about, a dreaming
feature. When the machine sits idle, the
memory reorganizes itself, cleans up,
links what should be linked, the way
your brain consolidates while you sleep.
So, it is getting better at remembering
while you are not even using it. Here's
what I keep coming back to. A model on
your own machine is already great,
private, yours. Nothing leaves the box.
But, without memory, it is still a
stranger. Give it a memory that follows
you around, one that lives on your disk
as plain markdown you can open and read
yourself, and it stops being a generic
chatbot. It starts being your AI, one
that knows you across every harness.
Running it locally is only half of it.
The other half is owning what it knows
about you. We took back the model, the
hardware, the privacy. Memory is the
next thing to take back. The whole
project is open, built on Karpathy's LLM
Wiki and Google's OKR spec. Links in the
description. Clone it, plug it into your
setup, and give your local AI a memory.
If you build something on top of it or
want to see a feature in it, tell me in
the comments, and I will see you in the
next one.

[END VERBATIM]

## نص فيديو: Aw7iQjKAX2k.ar.txt

[BEGIN VERBATIM]

تخيل أنك تدير
خط دعم للرعاية الصحية حيث يتصل المرضى
ومقدمو الخدمات
بأسئلة معقدة ومتعددة. هنا يأتي دور Graph RAG، فهو
يساعد في رسم خرائط العلاقات، مما
يوفر إجابات دقيقة ومخصصة بشكل
أسرع، وهذا أمر بالغ الأهمية حيث تُعد
الدقة والسرعة أساسيتين. اليوم، سنلقي
نظرة على كيفية مساعدة Graph RAG
في تقديم دقة أعلى وإجابات
أكثر شمولاً، بالإضافة إلى تسهيل التطوير
والصيانة وتعزيز الحوكمة.
سنستعرض ماهية Graph RAG
ونكشف عن فوائده
مقارنةً بـ RAG التقليدي في
التطوير
والإنتاج
والحوكمة. لفهم Graph RAG،
دعونا أولاً نشرح كيفية
عمل Baseline Graph. نبدأ
بمجموعة بيانات خاصة - يمكن أن تكون منظمة أو
غير منظمة - وهذا هو نموذجنا
التقليدي. نقسمها إلى
أجزاء نصية
ونخزن هذه التضمينات في
قاعدة بيانات متجهة. عندما نريد
استعلامًا، نستخدم قاعدة البيانات المتجهة
لاستخراج السياق، ثم نرسل
هذا السياق إلى LLM الخاص بنا، والذي بدوره
يقدم الإجابة.
جميعنا نعرف كيف يعمل RAG التقليدي. أما
Graph RAG، فهو مبني على ذلك.
نبدأ بالاستفادة من نفس
أجزاء Deex، ولكن بالإضافة إلى ذلك،
نستخرج الكيانات أيضًا.  والمزيد من المعلومات ذات الصلة
لتمكين رسم هذه
المعلومات في
مخطط معرفي. بهذه الطريقة، لا يكتفي Graph Rack
باسترجاع إجابات معزولة، بل يربط
المعلومات ذات الصلة، مما يُحسّن
جودة الاستجابات ويضيف دقةً وفهمًا أعمق.
لنأخذ مثالًا
لتوضيح إمكانيات Graph
Rack. لنفترض أن لدينا جملة كهذه: "
ناقش عالم مناعة استراتيجيات الاستجابة للفيروسات
مع الرئيس التنفيذي لشركة رعاية صحية".
قد يكون تحليل النصوص التقليدي قد
اكتشف عالم المناعة والرئيس التنفيذي
ككيانات مُسماة، لكن Graph Rack يتجاوز ذلك
بتحديد ورسم
العلاقات بين هذه
الكيانات، مما يوفر
سياقًا أعمق وفهمًا أعمق
لتفاعلهما. لذا، يُدرك Graph Rack
أن عالم المناعة
مرتبط ارتباطًا وثيقًا بعلم المناعة
والبحث الطبي، بينما الرئيس التنفيذي لديه
صلة غير مباشرة ولكنها ذات صلة من خلال
قراءته في شركة الرعاية الصحية.
يتجاوز هذا التحليل مجرد
ملاحظة التواجد المشترك، حيث يُحدد LLM
قوة وطبيعة هذه
العلاقات، مما يُتيح إنشاء
رسوم بيانية مُرجّحة تكشف عن أنماط F الداخلية،
مُحوّلاً البيانات إلى
مخطط معرفي. يُنشئ المخطط المعرفي متعدد الطبقات شبكة من
الكيانات المتصلة والمترابطة،
ثم يدعم المخطط المعرفي متعدد الطبقات
مجموعة واسعة من التطبيقات، بدءًا من
توليد أسئلة مُستهدفة وصولًا إلى
صياغة معلومات غنية و  تُقدّم الملخصات ذات الصلة بالسياق رؤى معمقة لا
يُمكن لـ GraphRack التقليدي
تحقيقها
بمفرده. لذا، وبالعودة إلى
تطوير الإنتاج وحوكمته،
يُوفّر GraphRack إجابات أكثر دقة
وشمولية في
وقت قياسي. من منظور التطوير،
بمجرد إنشاء الرسم البياني، يُصبح الحفاظ عليه أسهل من
GraphRack التقليدي،

## نص فيديو: JCAe1x68jW0.en.txt

[BEGIN VERBATIM]

On July 24th, there were two
releases on the same day.
Neither team
mentioned the other.  Anthropic
released Claude Opus 5.
Google Cloud released OKF
version 0.2.  Together they
answer a
question that has been open since
April.  Where the agent
stores what
your company knows.  This
pattern already had a name.
Karpatiy called this LLM-
wiki in a post
published on
April 4.  OKF is the format
in which this wiki lives.
Opus 5 is a tool
for reading and
writing it.  One format,
one
reading tool.  This pair is
the architecture, and for
the most part it's
just Markdown in a folder.
Creating this in an
obvious way
runs into three
obstacles.  I want to
show you all three.
Obstacle number one: a
million
token window is not a place to
dump your wiki.
Obstacle two: there is
research that agent-
written context files
degrade
agent performance.
Obstacle three: your
agent reports an
income figure.
Prove that he
fulfilled the request to
finance, and did not
come up with his own.  Version
0.2 answers two of
them in the headers.  Opus 5
answers the first one.
Let's start with the reader, because
its specifications
changed the design.  Opus 5
comes with a
context window of 1
million tokens.  And
here's the detail that
matters.  1 million
is both the default value
and the
maximum.  There is no smaller
option to
switch to
.  $5 per
million tokens for
entry, $25 for exit.  Same
price as the model it
replaces.
Anthropic reports
96% on S.Bench and a fixed
price for long
context.  So a request
for 900,000 tokens
costs the same per
token as a request for 9,000. The
“think” mode
is enabled by
default.  Now,
instead of a switch, there is a
five-level effort regulator.
Low, medium,
high, very high
, max;  high—this is the
starting point.  Depth
is what you buy
for each request in
tokens.
Performance indicators are the
most interesting part.
The trading firm
calculated that Opus 5
achieved a better
result,
using
about a seventh of the
reasoning tokens of the
previous Opus with
less than half the
latency.  The legal
team reported the
same quality with 26
% fewer
tokens at the
maximum
reasoning level.  Box
measured an 8% improvement
overall and a 17% improvement in
due diligence performance.
A favorite example of
Anthropic is a task where
models were given
a drawing without
the ability
to see it.  So she
wrote a
computer vision pipeline,
extracted geometry from the
raw pixels, and
recreated the detail.
It also scored 2.3
on the
non-compliance audit—the
lowest score
among all recent
Claudes with the lowest
level of deceptive
behavior.  But the line
that changed my
view of this
architecture came
from DataDog.  Their
monitoring agents
now manage
parts of their own
memory in industrial
operation.  One of
them flagged a possible
anomaly, tested
his own assumption
against the production
environment, found
that the signal was
safe, wrote
the correction to his
memory, and withdrew
his own requests.  They
described an agent that
treats its
context as a
living document.  This is a
wiki maintained by
those who read it, which
is the main idea, and in
a minute—the whole
problem.    The
memory tool
does this literally.
Claude gets
a directory called /memories that
he can view,
create,
edit, and
delete.  And the API
implements a constant
instruction.
Allow for
interruptions.  Your
context window can
be reset at any
time.  So, a
million tokens and an
agent who writes.
The obvious step is
to load the entire
company wiki on
every call.  This is the
first wall.  In July
2025, Chroma
published
a study
called "
Context Rotting."  18
advanced models.
The tasks were kept
intentionally simple.
One variable that
was changed was the length of the
input data.  Each
model deteriorated
as the
input data increased, not with a
sharp break at the edge of
the window, but with a steady
slide all the way through
.
Stanford and Berkeley
have already discovered a more pungent
version of this.  If
you place the desired
model fact in
the middle of a long
context, the accuracy
drops by more than 30%.
So, the window is a
budget, not a bucket.
Chroma's conclusion was that it's
not
whether
the information is there, but how
it's presented that matters.
There is a bill for
a million input
tokens on Opus 5: that's
$5 not per day, but
per call.
Do 100
agent calls a day, and that's
$500 a day,
about $15,000 a month
—mostly for
rereading the same
wiki you read
yesterday.  Instead,
read the index plus
five concepts.
Let's say 12,000 tokens,
and the same challenge
costs six cents.    The same
knowledge is
about 80 times
cheaper.  Caching
narrows the gap, but does not
close it.
Cache hits
are charged at
a tenth of the
input price, so the "
all in context" version
still costs 50 cents
per call versus the 6
cents that
the format actually requires.  OKF is not a
service, a database,
or a
runtime environment.  A
knowledge package is a directory of
markdown files, where one
file represents one
concept: a table,
a metric, a guide, an
API endpoint.  The
file path is
the identity of
the concept.  Tables/orders.md
is the concept of table/orders.
Your folder structure
is a namespace.
Each file is a YAML
header over the
main markdown
content.
Exactly one field is required, and it is of
type—a short string,
such as "big query table" or "
metric".  This is the entire
mandatory surface of
the specification.
No scheme registry,
no SDK, no
central authority.
The specification
lays it out in one
line.  If you can
open a file via
cat, you can
read OKF, and if you
can clone
a repository via git
clone, you can
deploy it.  We've
tried a more complex
version of this before.
OWL and RDF contain
typed
relations and
formal logical
inference, but they
also require
schema registries and
ontology engineers,
so their implementation

[BEGIN VERBATIM]

Hi folks, it's Mike Murphy. In this tutorial, I'm going to show you how to build an AI self-organizing second brain in Obsidian using Claude Code.
The AI powered second brain, or personal knowledge base that we are going to build today from scratch,
was inspired by the wildly popular X-post by Andrei Karpathy, which at the time of this tutorial has over 19 million views.
Well it turns out a lot of people, including myself, really loved Karpathy's approach to building LLM knowledge bases, or LLM wikis as Andrei refers to them.
And to make it incredibly easy for you, me, and anyone who read his X-post that wanted to build their own LLM knowledge base,
Well Andrei created this github gist called LLM wiki, which is basically the exact pattern or the recipe for building your own LLM knowledge base.
The prerequisites, or the tools required in order for you to be able to follow along in today's tutorial and build your own LLM second brain,
or your Karpathy inspired personal knowledge base wiki, you will need a link to the LLM github gist, which you will find in the description of this video.
You will need to be on either the Claude Pro or the Claude Max plan since we are going to be using Claude Code to build out the personal wiki.
If you haven't already done so, you will need to install the free and awesome Obsidian app on your computer.
To be able to launch Claude Code right inside of Obsidian, I'll show you how to get the free community plugin called Terminal.
And finally, to make it easy to save articles and things from the internet to your LLM wiki, you'll definitely want to install the Obsidian Web Clipper in your browser.
The big deal about the Karpathy LLM knowledge base that we are building today is that it is persistent.
Meaning the LLM Claude code in our case is constantly updating, fixing and improving our knowledge base.
So the more information we get it, the better our knowledge base becomes.
Here is a sneak peek or a preview of the LLM knowledge base second brain wiki that we are going to be building today.
Very simple setup.
There are three folders raw templates and wiki and then a Claude.md file, which are the instructions for the knowledge base.
The raw folder is like the inbox of your knowledge base.
This is where you dump all of the source material that you want to be added to your knowledge base.
And you can add just about any type of file that you want in the raw folder.
You can add images, PDFs, Word documents, Excel documents, CSV files, Markdown files, anything that an LLM can read.
You can dump it in the raw folder and the source material in the raw folder is considered immutable.
Meaning it never changes or is never modified.
It always remains in its original state.
The typical workflow is that you add something to the raw folder so you can drag and drop on your computer.
You could use the obsidian web clipper any way that you get something into the raw folder.
And then you launch Claude code and you tell Claude code to ingest whatever it is that you put in the raw folder.
Ingest.
That's the name of the file.
And add to my wiki Claude code.
The LLM in my LLM knowledge base goes to the raw folder and analyzes the source document that I told it to ingest.
Claude is then going to try to extract as much data or information or knowledge from that source material.
So every time the LLM ingests raw material into the knowledge base.
Okay, what do I need to do with this information?
Does it require its own wiki page?

## نص فيديو: LPZh9BOjkQs.en.txt

[BEGIN VERBATIM]

[Submit subtitle corrections at criblate.com]
Imagine you happen across a short movie script that
describes a scene between a person and their AI assistant.
The script has what the person asks the AI, but the AI's response has been torn off.
Suppose you also have this powerful magical machine that can take
any text and provide a sensible prediction of what word comes next.
You could then finish the script by feeding in what you have to the machine,
seeing what it would predict to start the AI's answer,
and then repeating this over and over with a growing script completing the dialogue.
When you interact with a chatbot, this is exactly what's happening.
A large language model is a sophisticated mathematical function
that predicts what word comes next for any piece of text.
Instead of predicting one word with certainty, though,
what it does is assign a probability to all possible next words.
To build a chatbot, what you do is lay out some
text that describes an interaction between a user
and a hypothetical AI assistant, you add on whatever
the user types in as the first part of
the interaction, and then have the model repeatedly predict the next word that such a
hypothetical AI assistant would say in response, and that's what's presented to the user.
In doing this, the output tends to look a lot more natural if
you allow it to select less likely words along the way at random.
So what this means is even though the model itself is deterministic,
a given prompt typically gives a different answer each time it's run.
Models learn how to make these predictions by processing an enormous amount of text,
typically pulled from the internet.
For a standard human to read the amount of text that was used to train GPT-3,
for example, if they read non-stop 24-7, it would take over 2600 years.
Larger models since then train on much, much more.
You can think of training a little bit like tuning the dials on a big machine.
The way that a language model behaves is entirely determined by these
many different continuous values, usually called parameters or weights.
Changing those parameters will change the probabilities
that the model gives for the next word on a given input.
What puts the large in large language model is how
they can have hundreds of billions of these parameters.
No human ever deliberately sets those parameters.
Instead, they begin at random, meaning the model just outputs gibberish,
but they're repeatedly refined based on many example pieces of text.
One of these training examples could be just a handful of words,
or it could be thousands, but in either case, the way this works is to
pass in all but the last word from that example into the model and
compare the prediction that it makes with the true last word from the example.
An algorithm called backpropagation is used to tweak all of the parameters
in such a way that it makes the model a little more likely to choose
the true last word and a little less likely to choose all the others.
When you do this for many, many trillions of examples,
not only does the model start to give more accurate predictions on the training data,
but it also starts to make more reasonable predictions on text that it's never
seen before.
Given the huge number of parameters and the enormous amount of training data,
the scale of computation involved in training a large language model is mind-boggling.
To illustrate, imagine that you could perform one
billion additions and multiplications every single second.
How long do you think it would take for you to do all of the
operations involved in training the largest language models?
Do you think it would take a year?
Maybe something like 10,000 years?
The answer is actually much more than that.
It's well over 100 million years.
This is only part of the story, though.
This whole process is called pre-training.
The goal of auto-completing a random passage of text from the
internet is very different from the goal of being a good AI assistant.
To address this, chatbots undergo another type of training,
just as important, called reinforcement learning with human feedback.
Workers flag unhelpful or problematic predictions,
and their corrections further change the model's parameters,
making them more likely to give predictions that users prefer.
Looking back at the pre-training, though, this staggering amount of
computation is only made possible by using special computer chips that
are optimized for running many operations in parallel, known as GPUs.
However, not all language models can be easily parallelized.
Prior to 2017, most language models would process text one word at a time,
but then a team of researchers at Google introduced a new model known as the transformer.
Transformers don't read text from the start to the finish,
they soak it all in at once, in parallel.
The very first step inside a transformer, and most other language models for that matter,
is to associate each word with a long list of numbers.
The reason for this is that the training process only works with continuous values,
so you have to somehow encode language using numbers,
and each of these lists of numbers may somehow encode the meaning of the
corresponding word.
What makes transformers unique is their reliance
on a special operation known as attention.
This operation gives all of these lists of numbers a chance to talk to one another
and refine the meanings they encode based on the context around, all done in parallel.
For example, the numbers encoding the word bank might be changed based on the
context surrounding it to somehow encode the more specific notion of a riverbank.
Transformers typically also include a second type of operation known
as a feed-forward neural network, and this gives the model extra
capacity to store more patterns about language learned during training.
All of this data repeatedly flows through many different iterations of
these two fundamental operations, and as it does so,
the hope is that each list of numbers is enriched to encode whatever
information might be needed to make an accurate prediction of what word
follows in the passage.
At the end, one final function is performed on the last vector in this sequence,
which now has had a chance to be influenced by all the other context from the input text,
as well as everything the model learned during training,
to produce a prediction of the next word.
Again, the model's prediction looks like a probability for every possible next word.
Although researchers design the framework for how each of these steps work,
it's important to understand that the specific behavior is an emergent phenomenon
based on how those hundreds of billions of parameters are tuned during training.
This makes it incredibly challenging to determine
why the model makes the exact predictions that it does.
What you can see is that when you use large language model predictions to autocomplete
a prompt, the words that it generates are uncannily fluent, fascinating, and even useful.
If you're a new viewer and you're curious about more details on how
transformers and attention work, boy do I have some material for you.
One option is to jump into a series I made about deep learning,
where we visualize and motivate the details of attention and all the other steps
in a transformer.
Also, on my second channel I just posted a talk I gave a couple
months ago about this topic for the company TNG in Munich.
Sometimes I actually prefer the content I make as a casual talk rather than a produced
video, but I leave it up to you which one of these feels like the better follow-on.

[END VERBATIM]

ملفات تكوين معينة في Obsidian يتم
تتبعها بمرور الوقت أثناء إجراء التغييرات، ولا

داخل هذا المستودع، داخل

نقطة آمنة يمكنك
الرجوع إليها باستخدام Git.  ولدي بالفعل
فيديو مخصص هنا حول كيفية استخدام Git
و GitHub مع الذكاء الاصطناعي ولماذا من
المهم جدًا القيام بذلك.  لذا إذا كنت ترغب في

بالاطلاع على ذلك.
أود فقط أن أشير سريعًا إلى أننا
نريد التأكد من أن

أنشأا هذا الرابط كعقدة داخل
مخطط المعرفة هذا.  هذا
شكل خاص من أشكال ربط الويكي الذي

الرابط الذي سأدرجه في الوصف،

أملك Obsidian CLI وmarkdown basis و

عنك.  وبشكل أساسي، ما
